original.Description: Photopigment Photon Absorption and Isomerization denotes the admissible process-level arising in which a photopigment molecule absorbs a photon and undergoes a rapid quantized conformational change that converts electromagnetic input into a discrete chemical state difference. Within Level 3 this arising is not merely the existence of a photopigment object, but the initiating photochemical transduction regime through which an embedded chromophore enters an excited state and proceeds through ultrafast isomerization within a structured protein environment. The arising establishes the first biochemical signal-bearing state change that can be amplified, regulated, and integrated by downstream biochemical networks. Within SOMA this phenomenon is classified as a process because the ontological unit is the photon-triggered conversion event itself rather than the photopigment molecule considered independently. This arising provides the structural basis for phototransduction onset and marks the boundary at which physical photon interaction becomes chemically usable biochemical signaling without presupposing higher sensory or neural organization.

original.Description: Eye Optical Interface denote the admissible object-level arising of a multicellular optical system formed when specialized tissues are integrated into a coherent refraction and projection architecture linking the external light environment to the retinal surface. The arising is realized through organ-level anatomical integration, tissue morphogenetic precision, and stable coupling among transparent and enabling tissues, yielding an optical boundary unit that transforms continuous external light fields into a structured irradiance distribution on the retina without itself performing neural transduction or cognitive processing. Within SOMA this arising is classified as an object because the principal ontological unit is an identifiable multicellular optical interface with stable structural identity and boundary-mediating function. This arising establishes the optical projection infrastructure required for image formation on retinal tissue and for subsequent downstream sensory transduction.

Evidence.Reference: Optics and visual-system literature documenting how cornea, lens, iris, and enabling ocular tissues form an integrated projection system producing structured retinal irradiance maps.

Physiological optics frameworks explaining eye function as a bounded multicellular optical interface coupling external light fields to retinal sensory surfaces through refraction, focusing, and aperture control.

Experimental and clinical evidence showing that disruption of corneal curvature, lens transparency, alignment, or pupil control abolishes proper retinal image formation despite intact downstream neural tissue.

original.Description: Retinal Sampling Geometry and Ordered Visual Mapping denote the admissible pattern-level arising through which the visual surface of the retina becomes organized into a non-uniform yet systematically ordered sampling architecture that constrains how optical information is acquired and spatially related to visual coordinates. This arising is not reducible to the mere presence of photoreceptors or to optical input alone. It consists in a stable organizational pattern defined by receptor-density gradients, spatial anisotropy, layered retinal circuitry, local convergence ratios, region-specific acuity, and persistent correspondence relations between retinal loci and ordered visual-space structure. Through this patterned arrangement, different portions of the visual field are sampled with differing spatial resolution, sensitivity, and processing bias, while preserving an ordered map that can support downstream spatial coding and visual coordination. The arising therefore formalizes the retinal transition from simple light-sensitive tissue to a geometrically structured visual acquisition surface whose internal organization shapes perceptual precision, field distribution, and later neural interpretation.

Evidence.Reference: Retinal neuroscience literature documenting non-uniform photoreceptor distributions, layered retinal circuitry, and stable retinotopic mapping as determinants of spatial sampling structure.

Visual-system frameworks explaining retinal acquisition as a structured topographic sampling pattern that shapes resolution, anisotropy, and spatial information preservation before downstream neural processing.

Comparative, developmental, and experimental studies showing that changes in photoreceptor density, retinal layering, or topographic organization predictably alter spatial resolution and visual-field sampling constraints without changing the external optical field itself.

original.Description: Retinal Circuit Preprocessing denote the admissible pattern-level arising through which multicellular neural circuits within the retina transform photoreceptor-derived signals into structured output patterns before transmission to higher visual centers. Within Level 5 this arising is expressed as a stable circuit-level processing pattern including lateral inhibition, center-surround antagonism, gain adjustment, temporal filtering, and spatial differentiation that selectively enhances informative variation while suppressing redundancy and noise. The arising is realized through the interaction of retinal sampling geometry, specialized layered neural tissue organization, and inhibitory and excitatory signaling mechanisms, yielding a distributed preprocessing pattern that reshapes incoming irradiance-derived signals into contrast-sensitive and temporally modulated outputs. Within SOMA this arising is classified as a pattern because the principal ontological unit is a recurrent distributed organization of signal-transformation relations across retinal circuitry rather than a single retinal object or an isolated signaling event. This arising establishes the tissue-level visual preprocessing structure required for primary feature extraction, contrast enhancement, and early filtering prior to cortical or higher sensory integration.

Evidence.Reference: Retinal neuroscience literature documenting center-surround organization, lateral inhibition, adaptive gain control, and ganglion-cell output shaping within local retinal circuits.

Sensory-processing frameworks explaining retinal output as an early circuit-level preprocessing pattern that extracts contrast, temporal change, and spatial differentials before higher visual transmission.

Pharmacological, electrophysiological, and genetic perturbation studies showing that disruption of retinal interneuron circuits abolishes center-surround structure and contrast-sensitive preprocessing while leaving primary phototransduction largely intact.

original.Description: Retinal Ganglion Spike Encoding denote the admissible process-level arising through which graded membrane-potential patterns generated by retinal preprocessing circuits are converted into discrete action-potential sequences by ganglion cells. Within Level 5 this arising is expressed as a temporally organized transformation from analog synaptic input distributions to spike-based output streams suitable for axonal propagation, temporal multiplexing, and noise-resistant communication. The arising is realized through the interaction of retinal circuit preprocessing, membrane excitability and threshold dynamics, and synaptic coupling mechanisms that together generate discrete spike trains whose timing, rate, and synchrony carry visual information extracted at earlier retinal stages. Within SOMA this arising is classified as a process because the principal ontological unit is an active graded-to-discrete transformation unfolding in time rather than a static retinal structure or a persistent spatial pattern alone. This arising establishes the retinal output transition required to bridge local analog sensory preprocessing and downstream spike-based neural communication.

Evidence.Reference: Retinal and neural-coding literature documenting conversion of graded retinal signals into ganglion-cell spike trains used for reliable long-range visual transmission.
Neural-coding frameworks explaining spike generation as a thresholded temporal transformation that converts analog retinal preprocessing outputs into discrete communication sequences.

Electrophysiological and pharmacological studies showing that blocking action-potential generation abolishes effective retinal output transmission despite preservation of upstream graded visual preprocessing.
